title: DNA Projects, Surname Studies & Y-DNA Haplogroups

subChunks.title: Using Y-DNA, mtDNA, and Surname Projects for Deep Ancestry
subChunks.hookHtml: Autosomal DNA testing is powerful for recent genealogy — typically five to seven generations. For deeper ancestry, Y-DNA and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) testing offer a different kind of insight: Y-DNA follows the strict patrilineal line (father's father's father...) and is directly comparable between males who share the same surname; mtDNA follows the strict matrilineal line (mother's mother's mother...). Surname DNA projects — voluntary collaborative projects on FamilyTreeDNA coordinated by volunteer administrators — aggregate the results of dozens or hundreds of men sharing a surname, enabling researchers to test whether their family is genetically related to others of the same name. Understanding these tools, their power, and their limitations is essential for genealogical DNA research at the intermediate level.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Y-DNA — the patrilineal line

Y-DNA is passed from father to son with minimal recombination, accumulating occasional random mutations (STR repeats or SNP changes) over generations. These accumulated differences form a Y-DNA signature that can be used to:

  • Determine haplogroup: a broad genetic population group based on ancient SNP markers, indicating deep geographic ancestry (e.g., R1b for Western European, R1a for Eastern European/South Asian, E for Sub-Saharan African, J2 for Middle Eastern). Haplogroups indicate ancestry from tens of thousands of years ago — useful for deep ancestry but not for genealogical identification of specific ancestors.
  • Compare Y-STR haplotypes: short tandem repeat (STR) markers mutate faster than SNPs and can be used to assess how closely related two men are in the genealogical timeframe. Men who share a surname and have closely matching STR haplotypes are likely related within a genealogically traceable period (5–20 generations).
  • Big Y testing: FamilyTreeDNA's Big Y-700 test sequences the entire Y chromosome for SNP discovery, enabling fine-grained haplogroup placement and identification of private mutations specific to a family lineage.

Y-DNA is only directly available from biological males; women must test a male-line relative (father, brother, paternal uncle, male paternal cousin) to access their patrilineal Y-DNA.

Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) — the matrilineal line

mtDNA is passed from mother to all children (male and female) with minimal recombination. It accumulates mutations over thousands of years and can be used to:

  • Determine maternal haplogroup: similar to Y-DNA haplogroups but tracking the maternal line. Haplogroup H is the most common in Western Europe; haplogroup L indicates deep African maternal ancestry.
  • Full Sequence (FMS) testing: testing the full mitochondrial genome gives the highest resolution; exact sequence matches (genetic distance 0) indicate a shared maternal ancestor within a genealogically meaningful timeframe, though the exact number of generations cannot be determined from mtDNA alone.
  • Limitations: mtDNA mutates slowly; an exact match may indicate a shared ancestor 5 generations ago or 50 generations ago. It is most useful for confirming or disproving proposed matrilineal relationships and for deep ancestry analysis, not for connecting specific genealogical family members.

Unlike Y-DNA (which tracks a surname line), the matrilineal surname changes with each generation. Tracking a specific mtDNA line requires identifying the sequence of matrilineal surnames back through the generations.

Surname DNA projects

Surname DNA projects are collaborative voluntary projects hosted on FamilyTreeDNA (ftdna.com), coordinated by volunteer administrators. The structure:

  • Any surname can have a project; many have hundreds of participants.
  • Participants (males who carry that surname or test on behalf of a male-line relative) contribute their Y-DNA results.
  • The project administrator groups participants into family groups ('clusters') based on STR haplotype similarity.
  • A project with 200 Smith participants might identify 15 genetically distinct Smith families — confirming that the various Smith families derive from multiple unrelated origins, not a single founder.

Key uses of surname projects:

  1. Testing family oral traditions: 'Our family is descended from a specific Walsh family in County Clare' — test against other Walsh participants from that area. A close match confirms the tradition; no match refutes it.
  2. Finding NPE (non-paternity events): a man whose Y-DNA does not match other members of his expected surname group may have an NPE in the patrilineal line — a child born to a mother by a different father than the surname suggests.
  3. Extending the paper trail: if your documented tree reaches back to 1780 and another project member's tree traces a connected line back to 1680, a close Y-DNA match connects your research to theirs.

Haplogroup resources and tools

  • ISOGG Wiki (isogg.org): the International Society of Genetic Genealogy's wiki is the standard reference for Y-DNA and mtDNA haplogroup trees, SNP definitions, and testing platform comparisons.
  • YFull (yfull.com): an independent analysis service for Big Y results, placing testers on the most refined Y-DNA haplotree and calculating time to most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) estimates.
  • Haplogroup predictor tools: FTDNA's haplogroup predictor estimates likely haplogroup from STR results before SNP testing; useful for initial orientation.
  • DNA Painter: dnapainter.com — useful for chromosome mapping of autosomal DNA, but also has a shared cM probability calculator essential for relationship estimation.

Integrating DNA with documentary research

The critical principle: Y-DNA and mtDNA testing provides genetic evidence that complements but does not replace documentary research. A Y-DNA match between two men of the same surname who both descend (on paper) from the same 18th-century ancestor is strong corroborating evidence — but only if the documentary lineages are independently established. DNA alone cannot name the ancestors; it can only confirm or disconfirm proposed relationships derived from documents.

storyBeats.text: Theodora opens the FamilyTreeDNA Walsh surname project page — a table of DNA results with rows in different colours, each row a different man who shares the Walsh surname. Several genetic clusters are visible.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Look at this Walsh project — two hundred and forty men, all carrying the Walsh surname, all having tested their Y-DNA. And the project administrator has found twelve distinct genetic clusters. Twelve unrelated Walsh families. Some are descendants of the Norman Waleis family who came to Ireland in the 12th century. Some are anglicisations of Irish surnames. Some are Welsh immigrants. The surname Walsh is a single word that conceals twelve entirely different family origins. The DNA project tells you which Walsh you are.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Y-DNA follows the surname down the generations. Father to son, father to son, accumulating tiny mutations at each step. Two men who share a surname and whose Y-DNA matches closely are almost certainly descended from the same patrilineal ancestor within the last five to fifteen generations. If your paper trail reaches back to a Walsh in County Galway in 1780 and another project member's tree traces back to County Galway in 1700, and your Y-DNA is a close match — you have connected your research to his. His documented ancestors are candidates for yours.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And haplogroups — the deep ancestry markers. R1b tells you your patrilineal ancestors were in Western Europe tens of thousands of years ago. It does not tell you anything about your specific ancestors in the last five hundred years. Use haplogroups for context — for understanding where your family fit in the broad sweep of human prehistory. Use STR haplotypes and surname projects for genealogical connection. These are different tools answering different questions.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor Y-DNA and surname project concepts

Retrieve from memory:

  • What is the difference between a Y-DNA haplogroup and a Y-DNA STR haplotype, and what does each tell you?
  • What is a surname DNA project on FamilyTreeDNA and how is it structured?
  • What can Y-DNA match results reveal about an NPE (non-paternity event)?
  • Why can't mtDNA alone tell you how many generations ago you and a match share a maternal ancestor?
  • What is ISOGG Wiki and why is it important for genetic genealogists?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
A Y-DNA haplogroup is a broad population group defined by ancient SNP mutations accumulated over tens of thousands of years — it indicates deep geographic origin (e.g., R1b = Western European, J2 = Middle Eastern) and is not genealogically specific. A Y-DNA STR haplotype is a set of short tandem repeat values that mutate faster, making them useful for comparing relatedness in the genealogical timeframe (5–20 generations). Two men with closely matching STR haplotypes sharing a surname are likely related within a documentable period.

A surname DNA project on FamilyTreeDNA is a voluntary collaborative project for men sharing a surname. Participants test their Y-DNA and the administrator groups them into genetic clusters by STR haplotype similarity. The project identifies how many distinct origins the surname has and enables comparison between participants to find or confirm patrilineal relationships.

An NPE (non-paternity event) is revealed when a man's Y-DNA does not match others who share his surname and whose paper trail connects to a documented common patrilineal ancestor. The genetic evidence contradicts the expected patrilineal descent, indicating a biological father different from the documented one somewhere in the line.

mtDNA mutates very slowly compared to Y-STR markers. An exact mtDNA sequence match (genetic distance 0) may indicate a shared maternal ancestor 5 generations ago or 500 years ago — the mutation rate is too slow to distinguish short timeframes. Additional documentary evidence is needed to establish how recently the shared ancestor lived.

ISOGG Wiki (isogg.org), maintained by the International Society of Genetic Genealogy, is the standard reference for Y-DNA and mtDNA haplogroup trees, SNP naming conventions, and genetic genealogy testing platform comparisons — the go-to resource for haplogroup research.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Designing a Y-DNA research strategy

Your earliest documented male ancestor is Thomas Brennan, born c.1800 in County Roscommon, Ireland. You have found several other researchers also studying Brennan families from County Roscommon, but no documentary connection has been established. You want to use Y-DNA testing to test whether your Thomas Brennan and their Brennan families share a common ancestor.

Design a Y-DNA research strategy (250–350 words): what test you would take, what project you would join, what results would confirm or refute a connection, and what the limitations of the approach are.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — Take a Y-DNA STR test: Order a Y-DNA STR test from FamilyTreeDNA (the only major platform offering surname projects and STR testing). The Y-37 test is a minimum; Y-111 or Big Y-700 gives more precision for close relationships. The test requires a biological male Brennan in the direct patrilineal line (my father, brother, or I, if male).

Step 2 — Join the Brennan surname project: Search FTDNA's surname project directory for 'Brennan' (there is almost certainly a project given the surname's Irish prevalence). Join the project; the administrator will compare my results with existing participants and assign me to a genetic cluster if I match others.

Step 3 — Interpret results: (a) Close match (genetic distance 0–3 at Y-37) with another Brennan participant who traces their line to County Roscommon: strongly suggests a shared patrilineal ancestor in the genealogical period. If the other researcher's tree reaches back to 1750 in Roscommon, their documented ancestors are candidates for my Thomas Brennan's forebears. (b) No match with Roscommon Brennan participants: suggests my Thomas Brennan's patrilineal line either has an NPE somewhere, originates from a different Brennan cluster (a different unrelated Brennan origin), or the Roscommon participants in the project are too few to be representative.

Limitations: Y-DNA tests the single patrilineal line only; all other ancestral lines are invisible. A close match confirms a relationship but does not prove the specific connection — documentary corroboration is required. The Brennan project may have few County Roscommon participants, limiting comparisons. The number of generations since a shared ancestor cannot be precisely determined from STR results alone; Big Y-700 with YFull analysis provides TMRCA estimates but with wide confidence intervals.

Expected outcome: cluster assignment and a list of matches; the project administrator may have additional documentary resources.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend the difference between a Y-DNA haplogroup (like R1b) and matching Y-DNA STR results with another person — what each one tells you about your family history, and which is more useful for genealogy.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A set of short tandem repeat (STR) marker values on the Y chromosome, used to compare patrilineal relatedness in the genealogical timeframe — men with closely matching STR haplotypes sharing a surname likely descend from the same patrilineal ancestor within 5–20 generations.

A broad genetic population group defined by ancient SNP mutations — Y-DNA haplogroups (R1b for Western European, J2 for Middle Eastern, etc.) and mtDNA haplogroups track deep ancestral origins over tens of thousands of years, not specific genealogical relationships.

A voluntary collaborative Y-DNA project on FamilyTreeDNA where participants sharing a surname contribute Y-DNA results, allowing identification of distinct genetic family groups within the surname and comparison between related researchers.

A situation where a Y-DNA test reveals that a man's patrilineal descent does not match the expected surname group — indicating a biological father different from the documented one somewhere in the line (sometimes also called a 'misattributed paternity event').
The International Society of Genetic Genealogy's wiki (isogg.org) — the standard reference for Y-DNA and mtDNA haplogroup trees, SNP naming, and genetic genealogy platform comparisons.

questions.questionHtml: What does a Y-DNA haplogroup such as R1b tell a genealogist?
options: It indicates the deep geographic origin of the patrilineal line — R1b indicates Western European ancestry extending back tens of thousands of years — but it does not identify specific genealogical ancestors in the last few centuries
It confirms that the researcher is directly descended from a specific named historical individual within five generations
It identifies all DNA matches who share the same surname within the testing platform's database
It gives the approximate century in which the researcher's patrilineal ancestor migrated to their current country
questions.correctAnswer: It indicates the deep geographic origin of the patrilineal line — R1b indicates Western European ancestry extending back tens of thousands of years — but it does not identify specific genealogical ancestors in the last few centuries
questions.explanationHtml: Y-DNA haplogroups are defined by SNP mutations that occurred tens of thousands of years ago in specific ancestral populations. R1b, the most common haplogroup in Western Europe, indicates that the patrilineal line descends from the population that expanded into Western Europe after the last glacial maximum. This is useful for understanding broad prehistoric population movements but says nothing about genealogical ancestors in the documentary period (last 500–1000 years). For genealogical purposes, Y-DNA STR haplotypes — which mutate faster and can be compared between men of the same surname — are the relevant tool. Haplogroups provide context for the deep ancestry; STR haplotypes connect living relatives.

questions.questionHtml: You join the Smith surname DNA project on FamilyTreeDNA. Your Y-DNA results are placed in Cluster 3 of the project, which the administrator notes is 'associated with East Anglian origins.' Your documented Smith ancestors are from Suffolk. Three other Cluster 3 participants also trace their Smith line to Suffolk. What does this suggest?
options: Your patrilineal Smith line and the other Cluster 3 participants' Smith lines are almost certainly related within the genealogical period — the Y-DNA match plus the shared Suffolk geographical origin strongly suggests a shared patrilineal ancestor among the Suffolk Smith families; the other participants' documentary trees may extend your own research
The result is meaningless — genetic clusters in surname projects are not related to geographic origin
You are definitely descended from the same man as the other Cluster 3 participants; no further research is needed
The Cluster 3 placement proves that 'Smith' is a surname of East Anglian origin for your family line only
questions.correctAnswer: Your patrilineal Smith line and the other Cluster 3 participants' Smith lines are almost certainly related within the genealogical period — the Y-DNA match plus the shared Suffolk geographical origin strongly suggests a shared patrilineal ancestor among the Suffolk Smith families; the other participants' documentary trees may extend your own research
questions.explanationHtml: A Y-DNA match (close STR haplotype) combined with a shared geographic origin in documentary research is strong convergent evidence for a common patrilineal ancestor. The DNA match alone would suggest relationship; the shared Suffolk origin narrows it to a specific population and period. The practical genealogical action is to examine the documentary trees of the other Cluster 3 participants, comparing their earliest known Suffolk Smith ancestors against yours. If one participant's tree reaches 1720 in a specific Suffolk parish while yours reaches only 1800, and your Y-DNA matches closely, their documented ancestors in the 18th century are candidates for connection to your 1800 ancestor. This is how surname projects extend paper trails: convergence of genetic and documentary evidence pointing to the same geographic origin. The result is not proof of a specific connection — that requires documentary corroboration — but it is a productive hypothesis.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher discovers that her father's Y-DNA does not match any other participant in the Pearce surname project, even though his documented tree traces to a Pearce family in Devon for six generations. She concludes the Pearce surname project database is too small to be useful. Is this the most likely explanation?
options: Not necessarily — the non-match may indicate an NPE (non-paternity event) somewhere in the six-generation patrilineal line; if a son was fathered by a man other than the documented Pearce at any point, the current Y-DNA would not match the Pearce genetic cluster; this possibility should be investigated alongside the database size explanation
Yes — all genealogical DNA projects are too small to be useful unless they have over 1,000 participants
Yes — the Y-DNA test must have been conducted incorrectly; a retest will produce a match
No — non-matches in surname projects always indicate the researcher has the wrong surname entirely
questions.correctAnswer: Not necessarily — the non-match may indicate an NPE (non-paternity event) somewhere in the six-generation patrilineal line; if a son was fathered by a man other than the documented Pearce at any point, the current Y-DNA would not match the Pearce genetic cluster; this possibility should be investigated alongside the database size explanation
questions.explanationHtml: Two plausible explanations for a non-match: (1) the project database is genuinely too small — if only 10 Devon Pearce families have tested, they may not include the specific Pearce cluster the researcher belongs to; (2) an NPE exists somewhere in the six-generation patrilineal line — a son born to a Pearce woman but fathered by a different man would carry a different Y-DNA signature while retaining the Pearce surname. Both explanations should be considered. To distinguish them: check whether the project has any Pearce participants from Devon specifically (if yes and they don't match, an NPE is more likely); test additional male Pearce relatives from the same line to see if the non-match is consistent; and examine historical records for any irregularities in the patrilineal descent. An NPE is not uncommon in genealogy — historical non-paternity rates were significant — and the professional response is to document the genetic discrepancy and investigate its likely cause rather than dismissing the test result.
